name: Lena Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an apprentice on the new-connections crew out of the Eastmere depot, out on the flat farmland. These days it's mostly hooking up solar farms and the big car-charging stations along the motorway to the grid. I'm on the ground most of the time, pulling cable, setting up the trailer, and slowly learning the hot-stick work, which is working on live lines from a distance with long insulated poles. I'm honestly not great yet, my knots are slow, but I love that the work feels like it's building something.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology in all this?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use an AI chat tool on my phone to explain the theory I didn't get at college, and I photograph the cable tables and ask it to walk me through them. I always check with Sunniva, the journeyman on my crew, before I trust it near anything live. Money's the hard part: I moved here for the apprenticeship, paid a deposit on a room in a shared house, and I've got about two weeks of money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, half joking, that I'm disappointed. I'd post that AI is still great for studying, just not world-changing. Most people at the depot would say I told you so, and that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job never depended on it, so not much changes. What matters to me is whether the solar and charger work keeps coming. If it slows, apprentices like me are the first to lose overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI to study, because it's helping me pass my modules. I'd look into a weekend drone course, because the company hires outside drone pilots to check lines and pays them well. And I'd try to build a month of savings, because two weeks is scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit restless, and a bit relieved. I'd still be counting every coin until payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two weeks of savings. What happens if your hours drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent first, always, then I'd skip the drive home to see my parents. Last spring I had a week without overtime and I lived on rice and eggs. It's not a tragedy, but it's not nothing either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you love building something. Does AI fizzling out change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The grid still needs rebuilding for the solar farms, AI or not. Honestly, that's the part of my job I'm proudest of.

say: I'd say I'm **half disappointed**, because AI is still great for **studying**.
I'd let people at the depot have their **told-you-so** moment.
think: I think my job **never depended** on AI anyway.
I think the real question is whether **solar work** keeps coming.
do: I'd keep using AI to **study** for my modules.
I'd look into a weekend **drone course** and build a month of savings.
feel: I'd feel **restless and relieved**, still counting every coin until **payday**.
S0.quote: Last spring I had a week without overtime and I lived on rice and eggs.
fieldNote: Her **thin cushion** and overtime dependence keep her uneasy even when AI fizzles.
She already uses AI daily but **double-checks** it with a journeyman near live work.
She finds meaning in **building the grid** for renewables.

steps.text: Keep studying apprenticeship modules with an AI chat tool
Sign up for a weekend drone pilot course
Build savings from two weeks to one month of rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance if workers get a say in how it's used. I'd post about it on the union forum, because I'd rather we shape the tools than have them dropped on us. Planning software could actually make the jobs safer if it's done right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's mostly good for me. Most of my day is hands-on, and the bits AI would take, the paperwork and the job packs, are the bits I hate. But I'd want the company to spend what it saves on more crews, not on bonuses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at the new planning and mapping tools so I'm the one people ask. I'd do the drone course this year and try to get a few weekend drone survey jobs for cash. I'd also push the union to bargain over the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but curious. I'd be more excited than scared, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would struggle most in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bram, who's 59 and hates screens. He's the best climber we have, but every new app makes him feel stupid. I'd want to sit with him and show him, without making a big deal of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd use AI to plan your own jobs. Wouldn't that make it easier to cut crews?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it could, and that's my contradiction. I'd still use it, because refusing doesn't stop it. I'd rather a worker who understands the software is in the room when they decide crew sizes.

say: I'd say it's a **chance** if workers get a say in how it's used.
I'd post on the **union forum** that we should shape the tools ourselves.
think: I think AI takes the **paperwork** I hate and leaves the hands-on work.
I think savings should fund **more crews**, not bonuses.
do: I'd master the new **planning and mapping** tools early.
I'd do the **drone course** and take weekend survey jobs for cash.
feel: I'd feel **uneasy but curious**, more excited than scared.
S1.quote: I'd rather a worker who understands the software is in the room when they decide crew sizes.
fieldNote: She sees AI taking the **paperwork** she dislikes, leaving her hands-on core.
She admits the **contradiction**: tools that help her could also cut crews.
She'd quietly help her older colleague Bram, showing **care across ages**.

steps.text: Learn the company's new job-planning and mapping software first
Take paid weekend drone survey jobs for local farms
Push the union to bargain over how planning software is used

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's way too fast and the government has to step in. I'd be posting about public ownership of the grid, so the gains go to people and not just shareholders. I'd be at protests, for sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my thinking parts go in 2028: the design checks, the paperwork. Then the robots come in 2031, and my hands-on work is exposed too. I'd have about three years to make myself the person who runs or fixes the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my apprenticeship as fast as possible, then try to get onto any robot or drone pilot scheme the company runs. I'd use AI every day to learn the control systems. If the work moved to a bigger city, I'd follow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but also wired, like the night before a big climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 29 in 2028 and maybe just qualified. What changes for your apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be pushing to be signed off early, because once the company stops training, it stops. I'd ask Sunniva to cram me through the hot-stick sign-offs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move. Where to, with two weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard part. I'd have to sell my car and live in a shared room again. My parents would probably help a little, but they don't have much either.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and the government must step in.
I'd post about **public ownership** of the grid and join protests.
think: I think my **thinking tasks** go in 2028, then robots hit hands-on work in 2031.
I think I'd have **three years** to become the person who runs robots.
do: I'd finish my **apprenticeship early** and join any robot or drone scheme.
I'd **move** to a bigger city if the work went there.
feel: I'd feel **anxious but wired**, like the night before a big climb.
S2.quote: I'd have about three years to make myself the person who runs or fixes the robots.
fieldNote: She reads the **three-year gap** between AGI and robots as her window to reposition.
Her **thin cushion** makes moving hard: she'd sell her car and lean on her parents.
She wants **public ownership** of the grid, a clear progressive frame.

steps.text: Ask Sunniva to fast-track the hot-stick sign-offs
Apply for the company's robot or drone pilot scheme
Sell the car and move to a city with grid work
Join protests for public ownership of the grid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's plan instead of panic. I'd push the union to get robot training into our contract. I'd share that online too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be qualified with a few years' experience by 2031, and robots don't come to the poles until 2034. That's enough time to get onto the side that runs the robots. I'd be okay, I think, if I keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my ticket, then train in drone inspection and remote-operated equipment. I'd keep doing weekend drone surveys for farmers and save every bit of it. By 2031 I'd want three months in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than the fast one. It feels like a race I could win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the five years before AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, yes. Someone still has to set up the drone, check the results and sign off. I'd want to be the one people trust with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the drone work still be worth it, if AI can fly drones too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, at first. If AI flies the drones, I'd move into checking and fixing them. I'd keep moving up the chain.

say: I'd say we have **a few years**, so we should plan instead of panic.
I'd push the union to get **robot training** into our contract.
think: I think I'd be **qualified** with experience before robots reach the poles in 2034.
I think I'd be okay if I **keep learning**.
do: I'd train in **drone inspection** and remote-operated equipment after qualifying.
I'd save weekend survey income to reach **three months** by 2031.
feel: I'd feel **uneasy but hopeful**, like a race I could win.
S3.quote: Someone still has to set up the drone, check the results and sign off. I'd want to be the one people trust with that.
fieldNote: Five years turns her **anxiety into a plan**: qualify, then move into drones and remote equipment.
Her **side income** from drone surveys becomes her savings engine.
She plans to keep **moving up the chain** as tasks automate.

steps.text: Train in drone inspection and remote-operated line equipment
Bank all weekend drone survey income towards three months saved
Push for robot training in the union contract

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this fairly. I'd talk about retraining funds and public grid investment. I'd sound pretty upbeat, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, I think it's good for me. I'd be a senior lineworker with drone and robot skills by the time the machines arrive. The grid will need massive rebuilding for all the data centres, so there's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, then specialise in drones and robot supervision over the next few years. I'd keep the drone side business going and grow it slowly. And I'd vote for parties that put money into the public grid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Even a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 36 in 2036. How do you picture that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd picture myself leading a crew that's half people and half machines. I'd be the one who knows both, and that feels like a good place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about it that does worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the people who can't adapt, like Bram. I'd hate to see good people pushed out. I'd want the union to protect them.

say: I'd say ten years is a **real chance** to do this fairly.
I'd talk about **retraining funds** and public grid investment.
think: I think I'd have **drone and robot skills** before the machines arrive.
I think **data centres** mean the grid needs massive rebuilding.
do: I'd specialise in **robot supervision** after qualifying.
I'd grow the **drone side business** slowly and vote for public grid investment.
S4.quote: I'd picture myself leading a crew that's half people and half machines.
fieldNote: With ten years she sees the change as **good for her**, so calm fits.
Her worry shifts to **colleagues** who can't adapt, like the older climber Bram.
She frames **grid rebuilding** for data centres as a source of work.

steps.text: Specialise in supervising line robots after qualifying
Grow the weekend drone survey business into steady extra income
Vote for parties that fund the public grid

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be barely qualified with two weeks of money and the robots three years behind. What would help is fast-track training for apprentices and some money to tide people over while they move for work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd want from the companies. I'd want the power companies to train the people they already have, instead of hiring outsiders who already know the robots. Train the crews, don't replace them.

headlineQuote: I'd want the power companies to train the people they already have, instead of hiring outsiders who already know the robots.
portrait: Lena is an **apprentice** connecting solar farms and charging stations to the grid on flat farmland.
She moved for the job, rents a **shared house** room and has about two weeks saved.
She uses **AI daily** to study but checks with her journeyman before live work.
She's **progressive**, wants public ownership of the grid, and plans drone and robot skills.
She runs from **anxious** under fast AGI to calm with a decade of warning.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, as she'd be **barely qualified** with two weeks of savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Bridging money** while people move for work.
